motion: This House would abolish the minimum wage law.

args.text: In a labor market increasingly shaped by automation and digital platforms, a fixed minimum wage can accelerate substitution of low-skill tasks with software or machines by making marginal roles uneconomical. Abolishing the minimum wage allows wages for entry-level and transitional work to adjust to productivity, keeping more humans employed while they acquire skills that complement technology. It also enables platforms to offer flexible micro-tasks and training-linked compensation that can scale with measurable performance rather than a legally imposed floor.

Lower wages do not reliably prevent automation because adoption decisions are driven by scalability, quality control, and declining capital costs, so abolishing the minimum wage mainly shifts bargaining power toward platforms rather than preserving jobs. A wage floor can counteract algorithmic monopsony and information asymmetries in gig markets, where workers often cannot negotiate or verify productivity-based pay schemes. It also supports skill acquisition by stabilizing incomes so workers can invest time in training, instead of being locked into low-paid, high-churn micro-tasks that limit upward mobility.

Abolishing the minimum wage allows wages to reflect differences in productivity, local cost structures, and firm margins, which can increase the quantity of low-skill jobs offered and reduce rationing of work through reduced hours or stricter hiring. It can lower barriers for small firms and new entrants that cannot absorb a uniform wage floor, supporting business formation and competition that raise overall employment. Distributional goals are better achieved through taxes and transfers that supplement low incomes without pricing some workers out of the labor market.

Minimum wage floors mitigate employer monopsony and search frictions that otherwise depress pay below workers’ marginal product, so abolishing them can reduce incomes without generating the employment gains claimed. A uniform floor can be complemented by regional adjustments, but removing it shifts the adjustment burden onto workers through lower wages rather than onto firms through productivity, prices, or margins, and small-firm constraints are better handled with targeted tax relief than by permitting sub-living pay. Taxes and transfers can help, but they are politically and administratively incomplete, and relying on them risks subsidizing low-wage business models while increasing in-work poverty and reducing aggregate demand.

Minimum wage law centralizes a highly distributive decision in one national rule, which encourages symbolic politics and lobbying battles that often ignore local labor conditions and trade-offs. Abolishing it reduces regulatory power that can be captured by incumbents and organized interests to raise rivals’ labor costs, and it shifts the political focus toward transparent redistribution through the tax-and-transfer system debated in budget processes. This approach preserves democratic accountability by making income support an explicit fiscal choice rather than an implicit mandate on a subset of employers and workers.

Minimum wage law is a widely legible baseline that legislatures can adjust and voters can punish or reward, whereas shifting support to taxes and transfers increases reliance on annual budget bargaining that is more vulnerable to polarization, austerity cycles, and administrative exclusion. Abolishing the floor expands the domain of private wage-setting where workers have weaker voice and where local political capture can be stronger, so it does not reduce interest-group influence but relocates it to employer-dominated arenas. Politically, maintaining a minimum wage also signals a rights-based commitment that reduces pressure on local governments to compete for investment by tolerating ever-lower pay.

Abolishing the minimum wage is morally preferable because it respects the autonomy of adults to agree to work arrangements they judge beneficial, rather than having the state invalidate those choices on their behalf. A legal wage floor can exclude people with low current productivity, limited experience, disabilities, or irregular availability from lawful employment, which harms their dignity and opportunity to build skills through work. If society believes no one should live in poverty, the ethical responsibility should be shared through broad-based redistribution and services, not imposed as a prohibition that blocks mutually desired jobs.

Autonomy in contracting is morally incomplete when one side can credibly threaten homelessness or hunger, because consent under severe necessity is not meaningfully free. A minimum wage sets a basic constraint against exploitation and affirms equal moral worth by ensuring that full-time work cannot be compensated at a level that predictably fails to meet basic needs. The claim that a wage floor excludes low-productivity workers concedes that some jobs only exist by paying less than a decent minimum, and shifting the duty to taxes and transfers still permits employers to externalize the moral cost of underpaying onto the public.

Legally, a minimum wage is a blanket prohibition on certain voluntary employment contracts, and abolishing it restores greater freedom of contract while leaving intact core labor protections like workplace safety, anti-discrimination, and timely payment rules. The wage floor also drives substantial compliance costs, enforcement disputes, and litigation over exemptions, tip credits, on-call time, and misclassification, which can be reduced by removing the statutory price term and focusing enforcement on fraud and nonpayment. Where income adequacy is a legal objective, it is more coherently pursued through generally applicable tax-and-transfer entitlements rather than by conditioning the legality of work on a single mandated wage rate.

Legally, minimum wage law is not a mere price term but a public-policy constraint designed to counter structurally unequal bargaining power, and freedom of contract does not require the state to enforce agreements that predictably produce legally cognizable harms like destitution and dependence on public assistance. Abolition would not simplify the legal system so much as shift disputes into harder-to-administer doctrines and fact-intensive claims about coercion, unconscionability, retaliation, and misclassification, while weakening a clear benchmark that aids enforcement against wage theft and underpayment. Tax-and-transfer schemes are not a legal substitute because they are contingent, budget-sensitive entitlements that do not create an enforceable baseline duty on employers, whereas a wage floor supplies a uniform, justiciable standard for compliance and remedies.

Abolishing the minimum wage can reduce social exclusion by making it easier for employers to offer lawful entry-level roles to people with weak work histories, limited language skills, irregular caregiving schedules, or disabilities whose initial productivity may not match a statutory floor. It can also shrink informal and under-the-table work by widening the range of legal wage offers, improving visibility and access to protections like documented hours, references, and pathways into training. With poverty prevention handled through targeted transfers and services, society can separate the goal of income adequacy from the social goal of keeping more people connected to formal work and community life.

Lowering the legal wage floor may increase formal job counts, but it also normalizes very low pay that can deepen in-work poverty, housing instability, and social stratification even among people who are employed. The claim that transfers will prevent poverty ignores gaps in eligibility, take-up, and funding, so many workers will still experience material deprivation while employers capture the benefit of lower labor costs. Informal work is often driven by enforcement and immigration or scheduling constraints rather than the wage level alone, and removing the benchmark can make underpayment harder to detect and contest, weakening workers’ social standing and community participation.

Abolishing the minimum wage does not imply enforcing any bargain regardless of power; the law can still police coercion, retaliation, misclassification, and nonpayment while allowing wage terms to vary by role and productivity. The current floor creates hard boundary effects that encourage evasion and classification games, whereas a regime focused on accurate timekeeping, timely payment, and strong remedies for wage theft targets wrongful conduct without banning low-wage entry work. If income adequacy is treated as a legal right, it is more consistently delivered through enforceable, generally applicable benefits rather than by conditioning the legality of employment on a single wage term.

Relying on general doctrines like coercion or unconscionability is not a functional substitute for a wage floor because they are fact-intensive, costly to litigate, and rarely provide timely, predictable relief for routine underpayment. A statutory minimum wage supplies a clear, enforceable benchmark that strengthens timekeeping and wage-theft enforcement by making liability and damages easier to establish, whereas abolition increases ambiguity about what constitutes lawful pay absent explicit fraud. Treating income adequacy through benefits alone shifts the legal duty from employers to the state and leaves workers dependent on contingent eligibility and appropriations, which weakens the justiciable baseline that minimum wage law provides.

Economically, a statutory wage floor is a binding price control for some workers, so the adjustment commonly shows up as fewer hires, reduced hours, slower job creation, and substitution toward higher-skill labor or capital, even when measured average effects look small. Abolishing the minimum wage lets compensation bundles vary through wages, training, scheduling flexibility, and probationary pay that can bring marginal workers into formal employment and raise their lifetime earnings through earlier experience. If society wants higher disposable income for low earners, it is more efficient to use broad-based transfers or wage subsidies that do not discourage hiring and that can be targeted to household need rather than job type.

The claim that the minimum wage is a binding price control ignores that many low-wage labor markets exhibit employer market power and frictions, so a wage floor can raise pay with limited employment loss while reducing turnover and improving productivity, which offsets cost pressures that might otherwise show up in hours cuts. Allowing wages to fall in exchange for training or flexibility assumes workers can verify and bargain over those bundles, but in practice firms can re-label compensation as contingent, probationary, or discretionary while keeping effective pay low. Shifting income support to transfers or wage subsidies may reduce hiring disincentives on paper, but it also risks subsidizing low-wage business models and depends on consistent funding and high take-up, so abolition can raise in-work poverty even if employment rises marginally.

Morally, a minimum wage law treats some consensual work as illegitimate, even when it is a person’s best available route to experience, routine, and social participation. That prohibition can be especially harmful to those with lower current productivity or constrained schedules, because it blocks legal opportunities rather than expanding their real choices. If we believe no one should fall below a decent standard of living, the moral burden should be carried by society through transparent redistribution and services, not by banning agreements that would otherwise let people trade time for income and advancement.

Calling sub-minimum pay consensual ignores that many workers face urgent needs that severely limit their ability to refuse, so allowing wages to fall is morally closer to permitting coercion by circumstance than expanding choice. A minimum wage does not declare work illegitimate; it sets a baseline condition for lawful employment that reflects a duty not to profit from labor while paying predictably inadequate wages. Relying on redistribution alone weakens that duty by making the public finance the gap while employers capture the benefit, and it leaves many people exposed when benefits are incomplete or inaccessible.

Abolishing the minimum wage can reduce social exclusion by expanding the set of legal jobs that offer a first foothold for people with limited experience, interrupted work histories, or constraints like caregiving and variable availability. When the legal floor binds, employers often respond by raising screening standards or cutting entry roles, which concentrates opportunity among the most job-ready and leaves others disconnected from workplaces that provide routines, references, and social networks. If income adequacy is a social priority, it can be pursued more directly through household-based supports while keeping formal work accessible to more people at the margin.

Expanding access to jobs by allowing lower pay can increase formal attachment, but it can also widen a tier of work that does not cover basic living costs, which undermines social inclusion through housing instability, food insecurity, and higher stress even among the employed. Employers may still screen aggressively because turnover and reliability costs rise when wages are very low, so the marginal jobs created can be more precarious and less likely to deliver the stable routines and networks claimed. Relying on household-based supports to fill the gap is socially fragile because take-up is uneven and benefit levels fluctuate, leaving many workers effectively priced into poverty wages without a clear baseline.
